The test image shows a corn ear with large, irregular, brownish-gray tumor-like galls growing on/around the kernels. This affects the ear (seed/pod). Top candidates from the part index: Common_Smut, Head_Smut, and possibly ear rot diseases.

Let me view references one at a time, starting with my top candidates.
Common Smut reference shows white/silvery galls with dark spores. The test image galls are more brownish and irregular. Let me check Head_Smut.
Head Smut shows ear completely replaced by dark spore masses - different from the test image which still has visible kernels. Let me check ear rot diseases.
Diplodia Ear Rot doesn't match - no galls, just rotted kernels. Let me check more candidates.
Gibberella shows pink/red mold on husks - not matching. Let me check Trichoderma, Fusarium, Aspergillus, and revisit Common Smut.
Trichoderma shows dark green-blue mold on kernels - not matching. Let me check Fusarium and Aspergillus.
Fusarium shows white mold on individual kernels - not matching. Let me check Aspergillus and then revisit Common Smut with a different reference.
Aspergillus shows olive-green powdery mold - not matching. Now let me revisit Common Smut with its leaf reference, since it can affect any above-ground part.

I've now used all 8 reference image views across 8 different classes.

**Analysis:**

The test image shows a corn ear still on the plant with large, irregular, brownish-gray tumor-like galls growing among and around visible kernels. Key observations:

- **Galls on the ear**: Large, irregular masses growing between/around kernels
- **Brownish-gray color**: Consistent with mature Common Smut galls (past the white/silvery stage)
- **Kernels still visible**: The ear isn't completely replaced, ruling out Head Smut
- **No mold/powdery growth**: Rules out Fusarium, Aspergillus, Trichoderma, Gibberella
- **No white mycelium from base**: Rules out Diplodia Ear Rot

Common Smut (Ustilago maydis) produces galls on any above-ground part. The first reference showed white/silvery galls with dark spore masses on an ear - an earlier stage. The test image shows more mature galls that have turned brown/gray but haven't fully ruptured. Head Smut completely replaces the ear with dark spore masses and vascular strands, which doesn't match the partial gall formation with visible kernels seen here.
